rendered:
The review's reasoning rests on transport kinetics. The lithium-ion diffusivity of most oxides and fluorides is very low, and the review singles out ZrO2 as especially poor: is extremely low, particularly for ZrO2[1]

Lithium ions must cross the coating, so the diffusion time grows with coating thickness: longer diffusion times are observed for thicker coating layers[2]. As a result, the measured electrochemical performance is limited by ionic diffusion through the coating layer: ited by the ionic diffusion at the coating layer[3].

On that basis, the review's own calculation from its diffusion figure concludes that the ideal coating thickness is ideal thicknesses for these surface coatings should be below ten nanometers[4], well below the tens-of-nanometres range. For widely used cost-effective coatings, which exhibit very low lithium-ion diffusivity, the review gives a maximum thickness of around ∼10 nm for effective[5].

The tens-of-nanometres figure is therefore what the literature typically reports, not the recommended value: The reported coating thickness in literature, in most cases, is in the[6] tens of nanometers as it is difficult to be controlled by easily scalable[7].

The review also notes that thick coatings often still give good rate capability, which it says is not clearly explained in the literature: exhibit excellent rate capabilities despite the thickness of the[8].

A second reason for keeping coatings thin is chemical. Inert, stable oxides such as ZrO2 or Al2O3 may react with lithium ions and form secondary phases[9] (for example Li2ZrO3), resulting in capacity fading issue[10]. A thin layer limits how much of this reaction can occur, which is part of the case for minimal thickness.
